analysis.one_liner: Bans patents on surgical and medical procedures, therapies, and diagnoses.
analysis.headline: Despite 137 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never got a vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some inventors had patented ways of performing surgery or treating patients, which meant doctors and hospitals could owe royalties for using a technique. This bill would have stopped the government from issuing new patents on medical procedures, therapies, or diagnoses. It kept a carve-out: if the technique runs through a patented machine or device, the device patent could still cover it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and doctors. Patients would avoid royalties on techniques being added to the cost of care, and surgeons could use established and new methods without risking a patent-infringement lawsuit. Only patents issued after the law took effect would be blocked; the bill does not say it would void existing ones.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars new patents on any technique, method, or process for performing a surgical or medical procedure, administering a therapy, or making a diagnosis.
Doctors and hospitals would not owe royalties for the way they perform care, and a technique could be freely taught and used by other practitioners.

analysis.who_pays: Inventors, universities, and companies that hold or seek patents on medical techniques would lose that revenue stream, though any method performed through a patented machine or device remains protectable.

drawbacks.text: Patents are designed to reward invention: an inventor who develops a genuinely new surgical technique would no longer be able to patent the method itself and recoup the investment, which opponents argue could reduce the incentive to develop new techniques.

The carve-out for machines and devices means a company can still patent a device and claim the technique it performs, so some technique royalties could survive through the hardware rather than disappearing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and doctors, the benefits are direct: cheaper care and no infringement risk for the act of treating a patient. The honest cost is weaker patent protection for pure techniques, though the bill deliberately preserves full patent rights for machines, devices, and drugs, where most medical R&D incentives already sit. The design is a reasonable compromise rather than an extreme position, which is one reason it drew broad bipartisan support.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its intellectual property subcommittee, which held a hearing in October 1995; the bill never came back out of committee and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Ganske, a surgeon, introduced the bill with Rep. Ron Wyden on March 3, 1995.
It attracted 137 cosponsors — 109 Republicans, 27 Democrats, and 1 Independent.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property.
The subcommittee held hearings on October 19, 1995, but no further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Holders of medical procedure patents kept their exclusive rights and royalty streams, and the device industry kept its patent rights intact through the machine carve-out. Patients and surgeons gained nothing from this bill, though the problem it targeted was addressed by a different measure before the decade ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medical procedure patent holders and device makers

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily bipartisan: 109 of the 137 cosponsors were Republicans and 27 were Democrats, and the bill was introduced jointly by a Republican and a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would block new patents on medical techniques, ending royalty charges on the act of performing care. Their gain had come from charging doctors and hospitals for methods practitioners needed to treat patients.

The bill's carve-out lets a patent on a machine or device claim the technique it performs, so device makers keep their patent rights and can still price-protect their equipment even as pure technique patents are banned.
Surgeons and hospitals would no longer face infringement liability or royalties for using a patented method of surgery or diagnosis, lowering both their legal risk and the cost passed to patients.
